options.label: A single enormous star like the Sun
options.feedback: A star is a single object, not a system of many stars. A galaxy contains billions of stars.

options.label: A cloud of gas and dust floating in space
options.feedback: Gas and dust are part of a galaxy, but they don't make one alone. A galaxy is a huge collection of stars and other matter held together by gravity.

options.label: A huge system of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter held together by gravity
options.feedback: Correct. A galaxy is a vast gravitationally bound collection that includes stars, gas, dust, and dark matter.

options.label: A cluster of planets orbiting a central star
options.feedback: That describes a solar system, not a galaxy. A galaxy is far larger and contains many star systems.

items.ok_line: A galaxy is a huge gravitationally bound system of stars and other matter.
items.ko_line: A galaxy is much more than one star or a cloud.
items.exp_text: A galaxy is a massive, self-contained system of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter, all held together by gravity. It is far larger than any star or solar system, and can contain hundreds of billions of stars.

items.prompt: What shape does an elliptical galaxy have?

options.label: A flat disk with spiral arms
options.feedback: That is the shape of a spiral galaxy, not an elliptical one. Elliptical galaxies are round or oval and lack spiral arms.

options.label: A smooth, rounded or oval shape
options.feedback: Correct. Elliptical galaxies look like smooth, stretched spheres, with no flat disk or spiral structure.

options.label: An irregular, chaotic blob with no clear shape
options.feedback: That describes an irregular galaxy. Elliptical galaxies have a regular, smooth rounded form.

options.label: A thin ring of stars surrounding an empty center
options.feedback: Elliptical galaxies are filled with stars throughout, not hollow in the middle. They have no ring structure.

items.ok_line: Elliptical galaxies are smooth, rounded ovals of stars.
items.ko_line: Elliptical galaxies are not flat disks and not chaotic blobs.
items.exp_text: An elliptical galaxy is a smooth, rounded or oval collection of stars. Unlike spiral galaxies, it has no flat disk, no spiral arms, and no prominent gas or dust lanes.

items.prompt: What is the main visible component of a spiral galaxy that gives it its flat, disk-like appearance?

options.label: A thin, rotating disk of stars, gas, and dust
options.feedback: Correct. The disk is the flat part where spiral arms sit, made of stars and interstellar material.

options.label: A spherical halo of old stars
options.feedback: The halo is a round, diffuse region around the disk, not the flat part that defines the spiral shape.

options.label: A central bulge of tightly packed stars
options.feedback: The bulge is the dense center, but it is round or oval, not flat like the disk.

options.label: A network of dark matter filaments
options.feedback: Dark matter is invisible and not part of the visible disk. The disk is made of ordinary matter like stars and gas.

items.ok_line: The disk is the flat component that holds the spiral arms.
items.ko_line: Halo and bulge are round, not flat like the disk.
items.exp_text: A spiral galaxy looks flat because most of its stars, gas, and dust lie in a thin, rotating disk. The bulge is a round central concentration, and the halo is a sparse sphere around the whole galaxy.

items.prompt: Where is the Sun located within the Milky Way?

options.label: At the exact center of the galaxy
options.feedback: The Sun is far from the center. It orbits at a large distance, well out in the disk.

options.label: In the spherical halo, above the disk
options.feedback: The Sun lies inside the flat disk, not in the surrounding halo. It travels around the center along with other disk stars.

options.label: At the very edge of the galaxy's disk
options.feedback: The Sun is not at the outermost edge. It sits about halfway from the center to the edge.

options.label: Inside the disk, roughly halfway between the center and the outer edge
options.feedback: Correct. The Sun is in the disk, about 26,000 to 28,000 light-years from the galactic center, which is roughly halfway out.

items.ok_line: The Sun lies within the disk, about halfway out from the center.
items.ko_line: The Sun is neither central nor at the rim of the galaxy.
items.exp_text: The Sun is located in the disk of the Milky Way, at a distance of roughly 27,000 light-years from the central bulge. That puts it about halfway between the center and the outer edge of the disk.

items.prompt: What do spiral arms of a galaxy contain that makes them appear bright?

options.label: Only old, dim red stars
options.feedback: Old red stars are spread everywhere in the disk, but they don't make arms stand out. Spiral arms are bright because of young, hot, luminous stars.

options.label: Dark clouds of gas that block light
options.feedback: Those clouds make dark lanes, not bright arms. Spiral arms are bright because they contain glowing young stars and emission nebulae.

options.label: Young, hot, bright stars and glowing gas clouds
options.feedback: Correct. Spiral arms are rich in young massive stars and bright nebulae, which shine strongly and trace the arm shape.

options.label: A dense cluster of stars with no gas
options.feedback: Spiral arms have abundant gas and dust, not just stars. It's that material plus young stars that makes them glow.

items.ok_line: Young hot stars and glowing gas light up the spiral arms.
items.ko_title: Not old stars or dark gas
items.ko_line: Old stars are dim and dark clouds block light, not create brightness.
items.exp_text: Spiral arms look bright because they contain many young, massive, hot stars that shine blue and bright, along with glowing clouds of ionized gas. Those stars are short-lived, so they stay near where they formed, marking the arm pattern.

options.label: A small galaxy with only a few million to a few billion stars
options.feedback: Correct. Dwarf galaxies are much smaller than giants like the Milky Way, holding only a small fraction of the stars.

options.label: A galaxy that contains no stars at all
options.feedback: Every galaxy contains stars; a dwarf galaxy has fewer stars than a normal one, but still many millions.

options.label: A galaxy that is completely empty of gas and dust
options.feedback: Dwarf galaxies often contain gas and dust, especially irregular dwarfs. Their small size is about few stars, not absence of matter.

options.label: A galaxy that orbits a planet
options.feedback: Galaxies do not orbit planets. Dwarf galaxies can orbit a larger galaxy, like the Magellanic Clouds orbit the Milky Way.

items.ok_line: A dwarf galaxy is a small galaxy with far fewer stars than a giant one.
items.ko_line: Dwarf galaxies have stars and matter, just in small numbers.
items.exp_text: A dwarf galaxy is a small galaxy, typically containing only a few million to a few billion stars, compared to the hundreds of billions in a large spiral like the Milky Way. Many are companions to larger galaxies and are held by their gravity.

items.prompt: What holds a cluster of galaxies together?

options.label: The magnetic fields of the galaxies
options.feedback: Magnetic fields are too weak and local to bind whole clusters. Gravity is the force that holds them together.

options.label: The pressure of light from stars
options.feedback: Light pressure is negligible on cosmic scales and pushes outward, not inward. Gravity pulls galaxies together.

options.label: The rotation of a single giant central galaxy
options.feedback: There is no single central galaxy that spins the cluster around. The whole cluster is bound by the mutual gravity of all its members.

options.label: The mutual gravitational attraction among all the member galaxies
options.feedback: Correct. Each galaxy pulls on the others with gravity, and together they keep the cluster from flying apart.

items.ok_line: Gravity between galaxies holds a cluster together.
items.ko_line: Weak forces like magnetism or light pressure cannot bind galaxies.
items.exp_text: A galaxy cluster stays together because every galaxy's gravity attracts every other one. The combined gravitational pull of all the galaxies, plus dark matter, prevents them from drifting away from one another.

items.prompt: Which type of galaxy typically has the most ongoing star formation?

options.label: Elliptical galaxy
options.feedback: Elliptical galaxies contain mostly old stars and very little gas, so they form almost no new stars.

options.label: Dwarf spheroidal galaxy
options.feedback: These small, round galaxies are old and gas-poor, so they have essentially no new star formation.

options.label: Spiral galaxy
options.feedback: Correct. Spiral galaxies have abundant gas and dust in their disks, which fuel active star formation in the spiral arms.

options.label: A galaxy with no gas or dust
options.feedback: Without gas and dust, star formation cannot happen. Spiral galaxies have that material, which is why they form stars.

items.ok_line: Spiral galaxies, with their gas-rich disks, form stars actively.
items.ko_line: Elliptical galaxies have little gas, so star formation is rare.
items.exp_text: Spiral galaxies contain large amounts of cold gas and dust spread through their disks. That raw material collapses into new stars, especially along the bright spiral arms. Elliptical galaxies, by contrast, have used up most of their gas long ago and now form stars only very slowly or not at all.

items.prompt: What do irregular galaxies look like?

options.label: Perfectly round balls of stars
options.feedback: Round balls describe elliptical galaxies, not irregular ones. Irregular galaxies have no regular shape.

options.label: Patchy, asymmetric collections of stars with no clear disk or bulge
options.feedback: Correct. Irregular galaxies are chaotic, lumpy, and lack any defined spiral or elliptical form.

options.label: Flat spirals with well-defined arms
options.feedback: That is the shape of a spiral galaxy. Irregular galaxies have disrupted, messy structures.

options.label: Smooth ovals with a bright central nucleus
options.feedback: Smooth ovals describe ellipticals. Irregular galaxies are not smooth or symmetrical.

items.ok_line: Irregular galaxies are misshapen, clumpy, and asymmetric.
items.ko_line: Irregular galaxies lack the symmetry of spirals or ellipticals.
items.exp_text: Irregular galaxies have no clear disk, bulge, or symmetrical outline. They look patchy and irregular, often with scattered regions of star formation. This shape is usually the result of gravitational interactions or collisions that disrupt a once-regular galaxy.

items.prompt: What is the name of the force that keeps stars in a galaxy from flying apart?

options.label: Gravity
options.feedback: Correct. Gravity pulls every star and every bit of matter toward every other, binding the whole galaxy together.

options.label: Magnetism
options.feedback: Magnetic forces are far too weak to hold galaxies. They only affect charged particles locally, not entire star systems.

options.label: Centrifugal force
options.feedback: Centrifugal force pushes outward and would fling stars away, not hold them in. It's the balance against gravity that keeps orbits stable.

options.label: Electromagnetic radiation
options.feedback: Light and other radiation carry energy but exert only tiny pressure. Gravity is the overwhelming force that binds galaxies.

items.ko_line: Magnetism and radiation cannot bind a galaxy.
items.exp_text: Gravity is the fundamental force that attracts all masses to each other. In a galaxy, the combined gravity of all the stars, gas, dust, and dark matter keeps the system together and makes every star orbit the common center of mass.
